results.content:
AI made code cheap to write. Review stayed expensive. Every PR waited in the same queue, for the same few senior engineers. A renamed variable and a rewritten payment flow got the same amount of attention. Seniors became the bottleneck. They skimmed. Risky changes slipped through.

Today we are launching LiveReview: a risk-aware code review system built to fix exactly that.

Vote for LiveReview on Product Hunt →

If this problem is familiar, an upvote and a comment helps more engineering teams find this approach. It is the single best way to support this launch.

Watch the demo: LiveReview auto-approving a low-risk change while routing a risky change to a human reviewer.

## LiveReview auto-approves your safest 30-50% of pull requests [...] Every pull request gets a risk score. The lowest-risk 30-50% are approved automatically. The rest go to the right human, in the right order, ranked by how much they actually matter.

## How LiveReview differs from other AI reviewers

Most tools in this space pick one of two jobs: find issues, or check style. LiveReview is built to be the layer that decides whether a human needs to look at all, and ranks what matters when they do.

Here is what actually changes when you compare LiveReview against CodeRabbit, Greptile, SonarQube, Claude Code review, GitHub Copilot review, and Cursor Bugbot, feature by feature, not by marketing claim: [...] A security-first team can block on any security finding at all. A fast-moving startup can block only on correctness and UX bugs, and let style debt through for now. Both are one `jq` expression against the same findings document, whether the review came from the web UI, `git-lrc`, CI/CD, or the API.

# LiveReview: Risk-Aware AI Code Review for Business-Critical Systems

LiveReview is built for engineering teams that ship often, but also care about keeping production stable for customers. It approves some 40-50% of low-risk changes automatically, and it gives your team the tools to handle the rest: [...] How it works:

1. Track outcomes - trace production incidents and rollbacks back to the commits and reviews behind them.
2. Learn from the data - combine those outcomes with LLM analysis, static checks, and ML signals into a risk score per change.
3. Automate selectively - auto-approve the lowest-risk 30-50% of changes. Choose a conservative, balanced, or aggressive policy. Risky or uncertain changes still go to a human.
4. Keep improving - track incidents, false approvals, and overrides, and tighten or loosen the policy as real data comes in.

results.title: Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta: RADAR, Risk Calibration, and Review Efficiency
results.content:
RACER, Risk-Aware Code Editing and Refactoring, is Meta’s GenAI-powered tool for automating code changes at scale. RACER enables developers to delegate well-defined coding tasks, such as dead code removal, reducing cyclomatic complexity, framework migrations, lint fixes, and test generation, to an AI agent that generates diffs for human review. [...] For a diff to be auto-accepted, ACR requires a confidence score of at least 8 out of 10, with all changes classified into safe categories. If any risk signal is detected, the diff is automatically disqualified from auto-acceptance. This conservative acceptance criterion ensures that only changes with high confidence of safety proceed through the automated pipeline. [...] RACER also supports autonomous codebase maintenance through RACER Maintainer, which manages the full lifecycle of bulk code changes: discovering issues from code quality dashboards, creating tasks, generating diffs, assigning reviewers, and managing the diff queue. This mode is used for high-volume use cases such as cyclomatic complexity reduction, quality insight remediation, broken test fixes, and framework migrations.
RACER is relevant to RADAR because RACER-generated diffs are one of the primary sources of bot-authored diffs that enter the RADAR pipeline. When RACER runbooks are onboarded to RADAR, their diffs can be RADAR-reviewed and RADAR-landed through the ACE policy (Section 2.8) without requiring any human review, provided they pass all safety checks.

results.title: How auto-approving low-risk PRs with AI cut our lead time by 74% · Ona
results.content:
1. Fewer than 1,000 lines changed (additions and deletions combined)
2. No protobuf changes added or modified
3. No database migrations added or modified
4. No infrastructure or CI configuration changes
5. No authentication or authorization logic changes
6. No audit logging or monitoring changes

If any single criterion is not met, the change is routed to human review.

### How the review works

When a pull request is opened, the AI agent reviews it in an isolated environment with independent context. It evaluates the change against the low-risk criteria and code quality, then posts a structured comment:

Approved. The change meets all low-risk criteria. The comment explains the reasoning for each criterion. [...] Escalated to human review. One or more criteria are not met, or the agent flagged something worth a human look. The comment explains why and a label is added for tracking.

Auto-approve policy flow diagram

Every PR is reviewed by the AI agent. Low-risk PRs are approved automatically. All others are escalated. A human always merges.

### Governance

The AI agent can approve the review, but a person always clicks the merge button. That merge is the traceable approval event for SOC 2: the agent handles the review workload, the human controls what ships. The agent's review comment stays in version control alongside the merging engineer's identity and timestamp. [...] The engineering platform team owns the classification tooling. Any changes to the evaluation logic, the criteria, or the agent's review prompt require explicit approval from the Head of Product Design and Engineering. Swapping the AI model counts as a material change to the policy.

Auto-approve was the biggest lever, but we made two other changes at the same time: we stopped global auto-assignment of reviewers (which had created noise nobody acted on) and made PR authors responsible for choosing their own reviewers. The agent still reviews every PR regardless. For low-risk changes, its review is the only one needed. For everything else, it catches surface-level issues before the human reviewer opens the diff.
